title: CWP/28239/2023 of ISHWAR DEVI Vs STATE OF HARYANA AND ORS
judge: HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE HARPREET SINGH BRAR
text:
1 IN THE HIGH COURT OF PUNJAB AND HARYANA AT CHANDIGARH 237 CWP-28239-2023 Date of Decision: August 13, 2025 Ishwar Devi .....Petitioner VERSUS State of Haryana and others .....Respondents CORAM: HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE HARPREET SINGH BRAR Present : Mr. Som Nath Saini, Advocate for the petitioner. Mr. Piyush Khanna, Addl.AG, Haryana. Mr. Shubham Sharma, Advocate for Mr.Rajesh Gaur, Advocate for respondent No.4. HARPREET SINGH BRAR, J. (Oral)

1. The present writ petition has been filed under Article 226/227 of the Constitution of India with a prayer for issuance of writ in the nature of mandamus directing the respondents to make the payment of differential medical reimbursement amount amounting to Rs.10,58,338/- incurred by the petitioner on her treatment from different hospitals as she suffered multiple injuries in the accident on 03.08.2022.

2. Learned counsel for the petitioner inter alia contends that the petitioner was retired from the office of respondent No.4 after attaining the age of superannuation on 31.01.2012 and is getting her pension also from the said department. Further, on 03.08.2022, in the morning around 6.00 a.m. the petitioner met with an accident, from which, she suffered multiple injuries on her head as well as other parts of the body and a fracture on her left leg. Due to which, the condition of the petitioner was serious, as such, 2 was kept in Intensive Care Unit of Ravindra Hospital, Model Town, Panipat. Thereafter, the condition of the petitioner was deteriorating and keeping in view her serious condition, she was admitted to Max Super Speciality Hospital, Delhi. Admittedly, during her treatment, the petitioner remained in comma w.e.f. 07.08.2022 to 21.08.2022. Thereafter, due to fracture in leg of petitioner, she was referred to Max Smart Super Speciality Hospital Saket, New Delhi on 28.02.2022, where she remained w.e.f. 22.08.2022 to 25.08.2022. After discharge of the petitioner from said hospital she got admitted in Amrit Dhara My Hospital, Karnal for operation of her left leg and finally after surgery she was discharged from the hospital on 05.09.2022.

3. Learned counsel for petitioner further contends that after discharge of the petitioner from hospital, her medical record had been submitted before the concerned authorities for medical reimbursement. Further, learned counsel relies upon letter dated 08.05.2023 and emergency certificate dated 15.05.2023 (Annexures P-5 and P-6 respectively) and submits that the Civil Surgeon, Panipat vide Annexure P-6, had given opinion that ‘patient had suffered from RSA Head Trauma Cerebella Cartesian fractural Cartesian and she was declared as an emergency case on the basis of hospital records and treated at Artios Hospital, Panipat from 03.08.2022 to 06.08.2022. Similarly, vide (Annexure P-7) Civil Surgeon, Panipat given opinion that the petitioner was treated from 7.8.2022 to 22.8.2022 at Max Super Speciality Hospital Saket, New Delhi and further relies upon the judgment of Hon’ble Supreme Court in Shiva Kant Jha Versus Union of India passed in Writ Petition (C) No.694-2015, decided 3 on 13.04.2018, wherein it was held that during the treatment from the nonempanelled hospital, if found genuine reasons, the medical reimbursement of the amount spent on the treatment is required to be released. Further, learned counsel submits that urgency in admitting the patient in hospital, claim of petitioner cannot be denied because the hospital is not empanelled, as at that point of time the preservation of the human life was of the paramount consideration.

4. On the other hand, learned counsel for the respondentCorporation submits that out of five hospitals where the petitioner was remained under treatment, two hospitals namely Max Super Speciality Hospital, New Delhi and Artios Hospital, Panipat are not empanelled hospitals and as such, the case of the petitioner is not covered by the medical policy of the respondent-Corporation.

5. However, learned State counsel submits that the benefit of the observations made in Shiva Kant Jha’s case (supra) cannot be extended to the petitioner as the Court has clarified that the exception was created in the facts and circumstances of that particular case only. Further, it was made applicable to the Central Government employee, whereas the respondentCorporation is an autonomous body governed by its Board of Directors.

6. I have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the record with their able assistance.

7. It is not in dispute that unfortunately the petitioner had met with an accident in the morning of 03.08.2022 and had to remain admitted in different hospitals. The controversy in the present case is of non-payment of differential medical reimbursement because the petitioner had remained 4 admitted in two hospitals which were not empanelled. The hospital records’ were duly perused by the Civil Surgeon, Panipat and has given opinion that the condition of the petitioner was serious and it was the case of emergency (Annexure P-6 and P-7). In such a way, the test remains whether the claimant had actually undertaken treatment in an emergent condition as advised by the doctor to preserve the life of the claimant. The authorities concerned cannot deny the claim of the petitioner undertaken in the emergency. It is not the case of the respondents that the claim of the petitioner is not supported by the hospital record. The employer of the petitioner is in obligation to ensure the timely medical assistance. Admittedly, the petitioner is 69 years of age.

8. The claim for medical reimbursement ought not to be dismissed merely because the claimant underwent treatment in a non-empanelled. In such cases, the test of essentiality and emergency comes into play, which dictates that if the medical procedure was undergone by the claimant in an emergency, on the advice of a doctor based on her medical record, in order to save her life, the reimbursement for the same must be made. Not only is the preservation of human life instinctive, but it also forms a part of Article 21 of the Constitution of India, and therefore, it shall always retain the highest priority.

9. Moreover, the State bears an obligation to ensure the availability of timely medical care to those in need. As such, it cannot expect the citizens to refrain from availing timely care, merely for the reason of non-empanelment of the hospital. Such conduct on the part of the State does not satisfy the criteria of fairness and reasonableness and therefore, amounts 5 to a violation of the fundamental rights enshrined in Article 21 of the Constitution of India. Reliance in this regard can be placed on the judgments rendered by a two Judge bench of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Surjit Singh vs. State of Punjab and others(1996) 2 SCC 336,whereby, speaking through Justice M.M. Punchhi, the following was opined: “8. The policy, providing recognition for treatment of open heart surgery in the Escorts, specifically came to be examined by a Division Bench of the Punjab and Haryana High Court at Chandigarh in C.W.P. No. 13493 of 1992 titled as Sadhu R. Pall v. State of Punjab through Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Punjab, Civil Secretariat, Chandigarh and others, 1994(1) SCT 552 (P&H). decided on 6.10.1993, wherein the claim of the then writ petitioner to medical reimbursement was accepted when in order to save his life he had got himself operated upon in the Escorts, and the plea of the State that he could be paid rates as prevalent in the AIIMS was rejected. Special Leave Petition No. 22024 of 1995 against the said decision was dismissed by this Court on 2.2.1994. The other judgments of the High Court following the decision in Sadhu R. Pall's case are : (1) C.W.P. No. 18562 of 1992 decided on 10.5.95 titled K.L. Kohli v. State of Punjab and others, 1995(4) SCT 280 (P&H); (2) C.W.P. No. 260 of 1995, decided on 30.5.1995 titled Ravi Mohan Duggal v. State of Punjab and others (DB) (3) C.W.P. No. 5669 of 1994 decided on 4.9.94 titled Prem Singh Gill v. State of Punjab and others; (4) 1995(4) SCT 816 (P&H) : 1995 (III) Punjab Law Report 529 titled Tarlok Chander v. State of Punjab etc. (SB); and (5) 1996(2) SCT 148 (P&H) : 1995 (III), Punjab Law Reporter 682 titled Mrs. Surya Pandit v. State of Punjab and others (SB) xxx xxx xxx

10. It is otherwise important to bear in mind that self preservation of one's life is the necessary concomitant of the right to life enshrined in 6 Article 21 of the Constitution of India , fundamental in nature, sacred, precious and inviolable. The importance and validity of the duty and right to self-preservation has a species in the right of self defence in criminal law…

11. The appellant therefore had the right to take steps in self preservation. He did not have to stand in queue before the Medical Board, the manning and assembling of which, bare-facedly, makes its meetings difficult to happen. The appellant also did not have to stand in queue in the Government hospital of AIIMS and could go elsewhere to an alternate hospital as per policy. When the State itself has brought the Escorts on the recognised list, it is futile for it to contend that the appellant could in no event have gone to the Escorts and his claim cannot on that basis be allowed, on suppositions. We think to the contrary…”

10. In the matter at hand, the petitioner underwent surgery as well as remained on ventilator, which was necessary at that moment in order to save her life, as also depicted by her medical record. Therefore, the test of essentiality and emergency stands satisfied.

11. Accordingly, the present petition is disposed of. The respondent No.4/concerned authority is directed to make payment of differential medical reimbursement for the medical procedure undergone by her within a period of two months from the date of receiving a certified copy of this order.

12. Pending miscellaneous application(s), if any, shall also stands disposed of. (HARPREET SINGH BRAR) JUDGE August 13, 2025 P.C
